h1:
Burmese & Shan Food in Mae Sot
8 Spots Locals Love
intro: Mae Sot is a border town where food has crossed the line long before any of us were born. Here you'll eat Burmese, Shan, Mon and Karen cooking all mixed together in one city — something you won't easily find anywhere else in Thailand. We picked the spots where Mae Sot locals and Burmese workers actually eat, not the staged ones built for tourists, from clear-broth Burmese khao soi to fermented tea leaf salad to early-morning mohinga in the fresh market.

blocks.html: If you're coming to Mae Sot specifically to eat Burmese food, you've come to the right place. This town has real Burmese, Shan, Mon and Karen communities living here, and a lot of the restaurants are run by Burmese cooks making food the way it's made back home — not toned down to suit Thai palates until it loses its character. One thing to understand up front: Burmese food goes in a different direction from Thai food. More oil, a sourness that comes from fermented ingredients, and heavy on the spices. If you go in with an open mind, you'll get hooked.

We ranked these from real reviews on Tripadvisor, Wongnai and Lemon8, plus their reputation among locals. This isn't a strict best-to-worst list, because each spot shines on a different dish. It's more about which place to start with if it's your first time in Mae Sot.

blocks.text: 8 Burmese & Shan restaurants worth your time in Mae Sot

items.name: Borderline Tea Garden
items.blurb: A legendary Mae Sot spot run by a network of Shan women. You sit in a quiet garden with both tables and floor seating, and the staff are Burmese. The standouts are the tea leaf salad (laphet thoke), Burmese potato salad, Burmese curry over naan, and hot Burmese tea. Most things are very cheap, and the shop out front sells woven textiles and community crafts too.
items.meta: Open all day · on the Asia Highway, near the mosque

items.name: Lucky Tea Garden
items.blurb: A proper Burmese tea shop where a lot of people come for breakfast. The draw is the fresh oven-baked roti and naan, eaten with lentil curry or goat curry, plus sweet, milky Burmese tea. It's a simple roadside tea shop kind of feel — a good place to start the morning before heading out.
items.meta: Breakfast to late morning · in central Mae Sot

items.name: Mae Sot Municipal Fresh Market (Burmese breakfast zone)
items.blurb: If you want mohinga (Burmese fish noodle soup), Shan tofu noodles, or Mon-style khanom jeen, come to the fresh market in the morning. The stalls open very early and sell out fast. This is where Burmese people in Mae Sot actually eat every day, and it's the cheapest food on this list.
items.meta: Pre-dawn to late morning · town center

items.name: Mingalarbar Mae Sot
items.blurb: A Burmese restaurant that goes all in on home-style dishes — Burmese chicken curry, sour pork curry, tea leaf salad, and hot steamed rice. It's served as a set with several side dishes, like eating at a Burmese home. Great if you come with a group and order to share.

items.name: Burmese & Shan khao soi shops (market area)
items.blurb: Burmese khao soi isn't like the Chiang Mai version — the broth is clearer, there's no coconut milk, and the flavor is rounded out with beans and spices, topped with chicken or beef, fried shallots and lime. Shops like this are scattered around the market and the town streets. Just ask the Burmese folks nearby which one is best.
items.meta: Breakfast to lunch · market area in town

items.name: Shan curry & sticky rice shop
items.blurb: On the Shan side, the highlights are hang lay curry and fermented bean chili dip, eaten with sticky rice. The hang lay here has soft, fall-apart pork, and the curry paste is fragrant with ginger and tamarind, hitting sweet, salty and sour all at once. If you like northern Thai food you'll find it familiar — same roots.
items.meta: Lunch to dinner · a local shop in town

items.name: Tea leaf salad & Burmese fried snacks (Rim Moei Market)
items.blurb: Rim Moei Market right on the border has stalls selling fermented tea leaf salad, fried beans, Burmese samosas and other Burmese snacks to eat as you wander. Prices are easy on the wallet, so it's a good stop while you're browsing the souvenir market. Morning snacks sell out fast, but there's usually still some around mid-morning.
items.meta: Morning to afternoon · Rim Moei border market

items.name: Burmese tea shops in town
items.blurb: Tea shop culture is at the heart of Myanmar. Come sit and sip milky Burmese tea or coffee, eat Burmese fried dough sticks and sweets — it's where Burmese people sit and chat for hours. The vibe is relaxed and the prices are cheap, perfect for an afternoon break.
items.meta: Open all day · scattered around town

blocks.title: Before you go eat
blocks.html: Morning dishes like mohinga and Burmese khao soi often sell out before noon, so go early if you're serious about them · Many places are cash only and the staff don't speak much Thai — just point at the menu or the photos, no need to stress.

blocks.text: Burmese & Shan dishes you shouldn't miss

blocks.html: If you've never had Burmese food before, here's where to start so you order well and know what each dish tastes like.

items: Fermented tea leaf salad (laphet thoke) — fermented tea leaves tossed with fried beans, sesame, fried garlic and tomato, sour and savory with a crunchy bite. It's the dish people love most when you introduce a friend to Burmese food.
Mohinga — Burmese fish noodle soup, with a thick broth from fish and banana stem. It's considered Myanmar's national breakfast, eaten hot in the morning at the market.
Burmese khao soi — noodles in a clear, rounded broth from beans and spices, with no coconut milk like the northern Thai version. A totally different dish.
Hang lay curry — tender slow-cooked pork curry that's sweet, salty and sour, fragrant with ginger and tamarind. This one the Shan and northern Thais eat the same way.
Burmese roti/naan + bean curry — freshly baked bread dipped in lentil curry or meat curry. A filling, cheap breakfast.
Burmese samosas + fried snacks — crispy snacks you'll find at stalls and markets, easy to eat on the go.

blocks.text: Where to find Burmese food in Mae Sot

items.name: Central Mae Sot
items.blurb: Tea shops, Burmese khao soi shops and set-meal Burmese restaurants all clustered together, easy to reach on foot or by car. Good to base yourself here for several meals.

items.name: Municipal Fresh Market
items.blurb: The real morning-food zone — mohinga, Shan tofu noodles. Come early to find everything fresh and in stock.

items.name: Rim Moei Market (border)
items.blurb: Browse for souvenirs, then stop for Burmese fried snacks, tea leaf salad and roadside bites — pairs well with a border-area visit.

blocks.title: Straight from us
blocks.html: Don't expect fancy restaurants or fussy decor. The charm of Burmese food in Mae Sot is in the honesty and the home-style flavor. Some spots are little shacks but the food is excellent. If you can look past the way a place looks, you'll eat really well for very little money.

faq.q: Which Burmese restaurant in Mae Sot should I go to first?
faq.a: For a first visit, we'd point you to Borderline Tea Garden. It's a legendary spot in town with a nice atmosphere, a full Burmese menu of tea leaf salad, Burmese curry and Burmese tea, easy prices, and it's also a social enterprise supporting Shan women.

faq.q: How is Burmese food different from Thai and northern Thai food?
faq.a: Burmese food uses more oil, has a sourness from fermented ingredients like fermented tea leaves, and is heavier on spices. Shan food like hang lay curry, on the other hand, is very close to northern Thai food because they share cultural roots.

faq.q: Is Burmese khao soi the same as Chiang Mai khao soi?
faq.a: They're completely different. Burmese khao soi has a clear broth with no coconut milk, rounded out with beans and spices, while Chiang Mai khao soi is a rich coconut curry broth. If you're in Mae Sot, try the Burmese version — it's hard to find elsewhere.

faq.q: What time should I go for mohinga and Burmese breakfast food?
faq.a: Head to the municipal fresh market in the morning. The stalls open very early and breakfast dishes like mohinga and Shan tofu noodles tend to sell out before noon.

faq.q: Do Burmese restaurants in Mae Sot take cards or QR payments?
faq.a: Most are mainly cash, especially the market stalls and small shops. Bring cash and have small notes ready.
